blocks.text: Acts ends in Rome with Paul teaching openly from rented lodging despite being under guard. The narrative does not report the outcome of his trial or his death, so its ending leaves those later questions unanswered.

Rome is more than the final setting: Acts has earlier traced a geographic movement of witness from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria and outward. The closing picture of proclamation in Rome gives that movement its final narrative setting without requiring the story to narrate Paul’s later fate.

The abrupt ending has prompted debate. Acts is commonly discussed as ancient historiographic narrative, though it also invites comparison with biography, travel writing, institutional origins, and apologetic writing. Proposals for when it was written differ, and Paul’s fate after this chapter must be reconstructed, if at all, from later letters and reception traditions rather than from Acts itself.

Paul’s guarded lodging is the last stage of a longer Acts narrative involving arrest, military intervention, hearings, an appeal to Caesar, travel, and custody. This background helps explain why he can receive visitors and speak freely while still being constrained; it should not be used to treat every narrated procedure as an exact legal precedent or to portray imperial justice as uniformly benevolent.

The places named on the approach to Rome—Puteoli, the Forum of Appius, and the Three Taverns—fit a port-and-road corridor and help make sense of fellow believers meeting the travelers before they reach the city. Roman Jewish life also included communities, synagogues, Sabbath study, and ties to Jerusalem, giving concrete context for Paul’s meeting with Jewish leaders in Acts 28. These details do not make all Roman Jews a single, uniform group.

Paul’s residence should be pictured as guarded rented lodging, not automatically as a subterranean prison. No archaeological site securely identifies this lodging, and later Roman churches, prisons, tombs, and other memorials preserve later reception rather than independently locating the events of Acts 28. Roman urban housing ranged from elite homes to multi-storey apartment buildings, shops, workshops, warehouses, and other rented spaces; this broadens the possible setting for the visitors whom Paul receives.

The first-person plural language in this chapter belongs to a wider pattern in Acts 16, 20–21, and 27–28. Its source and what it implies about authorship remain disputed. Textual witnesses to Acts also include a substantially distinctive form often called the Western text, whose individual readings require case-by-case judgment.
